Borrowed from Middle Low German vinke (“finch”), from Old Saxon *fink (“finch”), from Proto-West Germanic *finki (“finch”), from Proto-Germanic *finkiz (“finch”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ping- (“small bird, sparrow”), probably imitative of a bird's call.

The chiefly plural culinary sense is also found in Danish finker (“dish of chopped meat and offal”), historically the plural of finke (“finch”). / Borrowed from Swedish finka (“prison; railway brake or heating van”), from Low German vinke (“prison”), attested in the compound vinkenbûr (“prison cage”), probably a humorous shortening of Middle Low German venknisse (“capture, captivity; prison”).
The latter contains the stem of vangen (“to catch, capture”) and the suffix -nisse (“abstract noun suffix”). The verbal element ultimately continues Proto-Germanic *fanhaną (“to catch”). One of several Norwegian spellings of a female given name going back to Latin Otilia, originally Odilia, a Latinised form of Old High German Odila and Otila, pet forms of names such as Oda. The Old High German names are formed from the Germanic name element reflected in *audaz (“wealth, riches”), with a pet-name or diminutive ending. The spelling with th is historical and does not represent a separate /θ/ sound in Norwegian.
Compare Danish Othelie, Swedish Othelie, German Ottilie and English Ottilie (“female given name”).
